transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Um, honestly, what finally made me come in is that I keep getting up during our really long sales strategy meetings at work. I know I’m supposed to just stay seated and listen, but I just... can't. I'll get up to refill my water, or I'll go pace by the printer. 

Which reminds me, our printer has been jamming constantly lately. It's this massive industrial thing and the toner is always low, so half the time I'm just standing there looking at a paper jam error code while my boss is presenting the quarterly projections. It's so frustrating because we do advertising sales, so we need high-quality pitch decks, and it always ruins the color on the logos. I actually had to apologize to a client last week because their brand colors looked completely washed out. 

But, um, yeah, even if it's just to get water or stand by that stupid printer, I just keep leaving my seat when I know I shouldn't be.
How long have you been having this difficulty staying in your seat during meetings? Has this been something you've struggled with since childhood, or is this more of a recent problem?

Oh, it's definitely not a recent thing. I remember this kind of stuff starting way before high school. Like, I was looking at my old report cards recently—my parents just moved to a smaller place, so they dumped all my old childhood boxes on me. It took up my entire trunk, and I had to sort through all these old macaroni art projects. 

But looking at the comments, my elementary school teachers used to write all the time that I was bright but that I rushed through things, and I always talked out of turn. And they'd always complain about my desk being completely stuffed with half-finished papers. I'd start a worksheet and just shove it in there. I actually still do that with my work notebooks, just starting a page and flipping to a new one. I love buying those Moleskine notebooks, the ones with the dotted grids? The paper quality is so good for sketching out ad layouts, especially when I use my nice gel pens. 

But, um... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, childhood. Yeah, the teachers also said I forgot my homework a lot back then, so struggling with this kind of stuff has definitely been going on pretty much my whole life.

You've mentioned difficulty staying seated and getting up during meetings. But I'm also hearing about rushing through things, starting tasks and not finishing them, and forgetting things. When you think about your typical day at work, which bothers you more—the urge to move around and get up, or the difficulty focusing and keeping track of things?

Um, honestly, I don't really know which one is worse. They just both kind of happen together. Like, if I think about my typical day... we have an open-plan office, which is supposed to be great for collaboration, right? That's what management said when they remodeled last year. They took down all the cubicles and put in these long communal desks made of this reclaimed wood. It looks super aesthetic, kind of like a fancy coffee shop, but the chairs they bought to go with them are incredibly uncomfortable. They have these weird metal backs that dig right into your spine. 

My coworker, Sarah, actually brought in a lumbar pillow from home just to deal with it. She got it at Target, I think. I love Target, I always go in for one thing like toothpaste and leave with a cart full of seasonal candles and throw blankets. Their fall collection right now is so good, they have this pumpkin chai one that smells amazing. 

But, um... yeah, so sitting in those chairs makes me want to get up even more, but then when I'm actually at the desk, I can't keep track of my client emails anyway because everyone is talking right next to me and I just lose my place. So... I'm not really sure which part bothers me more, to be honest.

When you're not in meetings—like when you're working at your desk on a task you actually need to focus on, or even at home in the evenings—do you still feel that same urge to get up and move around, or is it mainly something that happens when you're supposed to sit still in specific situations like meetings?

Well, I mean, it's definitely worse in those long sales strategy meetings. Like I said, that's what finally made me make this appointment—I just keep getting up when I know I'm supposed to stay seated. Even if I don't really need anything, I'll just get up to refill my water or pace by that awful printer. 

But at my desk, I guess I do it too. Like, I'll be trying to draft an email to a client, and suddenly I just have to stand up. Sometimes I'll walk over to the breakroom. We just got one of those fancy espresso machines, the ones where you put the pod in and it foams the milk for you? It's amazing. I've been drinking way too many lattes lately because of it. I tried switching to oat milk because someone told me it's better for the environment, but it just doesn't foam the same way, you know? It gets all thin and weird. I watched a whole YouTube video about how baristas get that perfect micro-foam, and apparently, it has to do with the protein content in the milk. 

But, um... yeah, so even when I'm just at my desk and supposed to be working, I still end up wandering off to make coffee or just pace around instead of staying in my seat like I should.

When you're working on something that actually interests you—like designing an ad layout or something you enjoy—do you still get that urge to jump up and move around, or can you usually sit and focus on it?

Well, if it's something I'm really into, like designing a layout, I can actually sit there for hours. Sometimes I forget to eat lunch when I'm doing that. But, um, if it's not something super engaging... like those long strategy meetings, or if I have to read through a dense client brief, it's totally different. I'll start out really focused, like I'm ready to dive in, but after a few minutes, I'll realize I've just been staring at the exact same slide or the same paragraph for ages. I'll have absolutely no idea what the last point was. 

It's so embarrassing when someone asks me a question about it right after. That happened with my manager, Greg, last week. He's always wearing these really loud, patterned ties. Like, who wears ties anymore, right? Especially in advertising. He had one with little golf clubs on it the other day. I don't even think he plays golf. My dad plays golf, though, he goes every Sunday morning with his buddies from the rotary club. He's been trying to get me to go with him, but it just seems so slow. Like, you hit the ball and then you just walk for ten minutes. I'd rather play tennis, you know?

But, wait, what was I talking about? Oh, the briefs. Yeah, if it's reading a brief or sitting in a strategy meeting, I just zone out completely and lose my place.

When you're relaxing at home in the evening—like watching TV or just sitting on the couch—do you find yourself fidgeting, bouncing your leg, or feeling restless, or are you pretty comfortable just sitting still?

Um, I'm not really sure, to be honest. I haven't really paid attention to whether I bounce my leg or fidget when I'm just on the couch. Usually, in the evenings, I'm just trying to catch up on shows. I just started watching that new baking competition on Netflix—the one where they have to make cakes that look like everyday objects? It is so wild. Last night someone made a cake that looked exactly like a pair of Crocs. Like, the rubber texture and everything was perfect. 

I actually bought a pair of Crocs last month, which I swore I would never, ever do because they're so ugly, but they really are incredibly comfortable. I just use them for taking my dog out. He's a terrier mix, I adopted him last year, and he gets the craziest zoomies right around 8 PM. We got him this squeaky toy that looks like a little taco, and he just runs laps around the coffee table squeaking it. I got the coffee table at a flea market, actually, and spent a whole weekend sanding it down and staining it this really pretty walnut color. 

But, um... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, about relaxing on the couch. Yeah, I don't really know if I feel restless or anything. I just kind of sit there and watch TV or play with the dog, so I haven't really noticed.

When you're doing something that doesn't interest you—like reading those client briefs or sitting through meetings—you mentioned you zone out and lose your place. How often does that happen? Like, are we talking about most of the time, or just occasionally?

Oh, it's pretty much every time. Most of the time, for sure. Like, whenever I'm in one of those longer strategy meetings or trying to get through a client brief, I really do start out focused. I sit down, I'm ready to work, but then literally just a few minutes later, I'll realize I've been staring at the exact same slide or the same paragraph on my screen for ages, and I have absolutely no idea what the last point was. 

It actually happened yesterday with a brief for this new client. They make these organic, vegan dog shampoos. Which is so funny because I was just talking about my dog! But honestly, dog shampoo is getting so expensive. I used to just use baby shampoo on him because my vet said it was gentle, but then I saw this TikTok saying the pH balance is all wrong for their skin. So now I buy this oatmeal stuff that smells like vanilla cookies. It smells so good I almost want to use it myself. Have you ever noticed how pet products always smell better than human stuff now? My own shampoo just smells like... soap. I tried this one brand last month that was supposed to smell like coconut and mango, but it honestly just smelled like a plastic pool toy. 

But, um... wait, I'm sorry, I completely lost my train of thought. What were we just talking about? Did I answer your question?

When you're doing something that you find genuinely interesting and engaging—like designing those ad layouts you mentioned—can you sit still and concentrate, or do you still feel that physical restlessness and need to get up and move around even then?

Oh, with the layouts? Yeah, if I'm really in the zone, I can usually stay put. But honestly, the whole sitting still thing... what actually made me come in to see you is that I keep getting up during those long sales strategy meetings. I know I’m supposed to stay seated, but I just can't. I'll get up to refill my water or just go pace by the printer. 

Which, oh my gosh, speaking of the printer, we just got this massive new one on our floor. It's supposed to be this super high-tech thing that collates and staples and whatever, but it jams literally every single day. My coworker Sarah spent like forty-five minutes yesterday trying to fix a paper jam and ended up getting black toner all over her brand new white blouse. Such a nightmare. I told her to try hairspray to get it out, because I read somewhere that hairspray gets ink out of clothes. Or wait, is that just for ballpoint pens? I don't even know. I used it on a couch cushion once when a pen exploded in my jeans pocket. It was this gorgeous mustard-yellow velvet couch I found on Facebook Marketplace. I was so mad. Velvet is so hard to clean anyway, you know? Like, you can't just use normal upholstery cleaner or it crushes the fibers and ruins the texture... 

But, um... wait. I'm doing it again, aren't I? What did you ask me? Something about the ad layouts?

Patient shows clear evidence of inattention symptoms (zoning out, losing place, difficulty focusing on non-preferred tasks) that occur consistently across situations. The hyperactivity-impulsivity component is less prominent and mainly situational (getting up in meetings). F90.1 (ADHD predominantly inattentive type) is now most likely, with F90.2 (ADHD combined type) still possible if hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms are more pervasive than currently apparent. The tangential speech and difficulty tracking conversation topics also support inattention presentation.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's primary difficulty is hyperactivity/restlessness (F90.1 - predominantly hyperactive-impulsive type) versus inattention (F90.2 - predominantly inattentive type). The patient has shown clear inattention symptoms (losing focus, zoning out, not remembering what was said) but has been tangential and hard to pin down on whether they have persistent physical restlessness even during non-demanding situations. This question targets the core distinguishing feature.
doctor.question: When you're doing something that you find genuinely interesting and engaging—like designing those ad layouts you mentioned—can you sit still and concentrate, or do you still feel that physical restlessness and need to get up and move around even then?

patient.answer:
Oh, with the layouts? Yeah, if I'm really in the zone, I can usually stay put. But honestly, the whole sitting still thing... what actually made me come in to see you is that I keep getting up during those long sales strategy meetings. I know I’m supposed to stay seated, but I just can't. I'll get up to refill my water or just go pace by the printer. 

Which, oh my gosh, speaking of the printer, we just got this massive new one on our floor. It's supposed to be this super high-tech thing that collates and staples and whatever, but it jams literally every single day. My coworker Sarah spent like forty-five minutes yesterday trying to fix a paper jam and ended up getting black toner all over her brand new white blouse. Such a nightmare. I told her to try hairspray to get it out, because I read somewhere that hairspray gets ink out of clothes. Or wait, is that just for ballpoint pens? I don't even know. I used it on a couch cushion once when a pen exploded in my jeans pocket. It was this gorgeous mustard-yellow velvet couch I found on Facebook Marketplace. I was so mad. Velvet is so hard to clean anyway, you know? Like, you can't just use normal upholstery cleaner or it crushes the fibers and ruins the texture... 

But, um... wait. I'm doing it again, aren't I? What did you ask me? Something about the ad layouts?

inference.note: Patient demonstrates clear ADHD presentation: lifelong history (since elementary school), difficulty sustaining attention on non-engaging tasks (client briefs, meetings), can hyperfocus on interesting activities (ad layouts), excessive talking/tangentiality throughout interview, difficulty organizing tasks (half-finished papers, disorganized notebooks), forgetfulness, and physical restlessness in situations requiring sustained attention. The tangential speech pattern and topic-jumping observed in this turn further supports ADHD diagnosis. F90.2 (hyperkinetic disorder) ruled out as patient shows primarily inattentive symptoms with secondary hyperactivity rather than predominantly hyperkinetic presentation.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a lifelong pattern of inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms that are pervasive across contexts (meetings, desk work, home), with onset in childhood (documented by elementary school teacher comments about rushing, talking out of turn, incomplete work, and forgetfulness). While hyperactivity manifests primarily as restlessness and difficulty remaining seated in non-engaging situations, the predominant presenting concern is inattention: difficulty sustaining focus on non-preferred tasks, frequent task-switching, losing track of information mid-task, and tangential thought patterns evident throughout the interview. The patient demonstrates capacity for sustained attention only on highly engaging activities (ad layouts), which is characteristic of ADHD. Functional impairment is evident in work performance (missed details, manager feedback). F90.1 (predominantly inattentive type) best fits the clinical presentation, as restlessness occurs primarily in structured/boring situations rather than pervasive hyperactivity.
